name: Decile rating

card.summary: A 1-to-10 scale where each point represents a tenth of the population, used to place a face or physique by percentile and set looksmaxxing goals.

quick.overview:
The decile rating is a way of rating attractiveness on a 1-to-10 scale, with each step representing a decile (a tenth) of the population. A 5 is roughly average and a 10 is among the top tenth. It is used to compare people to a population baseline instead of to models.

In looksmaxxing it helps people set targets for how far appearance changes might take them, and it is often discussed alongside PSL ratings.
quick.how: Members post photos for rating threads and explain how scores map to percentiles; one guide describes PSL and percentile ratings together, and others apply decile scores to celebrities.
quick.risks: Ratings from online strangers are subjective. Critics of rating culture, cited in media coverage of looksmaxxing, link it to body-image concerns.

lead: The decile rating or decile scale is a 1-to-10 system for rating physical attractiveness in which each number corresponds to a tenth of the population [1][3]. A 5 sits near the middle of the population, a 10 is among the top tenth, and a 1 among the bottom tenth, so the number is a statement about rank rather than a score of absolute beauty [3].

In looksmaxxing communities it is used beside the PSL scale, which rates male facial attractiveness on a roughly 1-to-8 hierarchy and was designed to reflect how women perceive men [2]. A looksmax.org rating guide describes PSL as originally comparing people with male models, places the average at 4, and gives percentile equivalents so that members can translate between the two systems [1].

For people trying to improve their appearance, the scale supplies a common yardstick: a member who posts photos can be told which tenth of the population he or she resembles, and can then ask which changes in skin, hair, body fat, grooming or facial structure might move that number. Published research on attractiveness ratings reports that raters agree with each other to a notable degree and describes which traits drive the ratings, which is the research most relevant to the idea [8].

chain: Rate face or body on a 1-10 population scale
Identify weaker areas such as skin, body fat, hair or facial harmony
Choose looksmaxxing changes and re-rate to track progress
angle.text: The decile scale gives users a shared number for where they stand relative to everyone else, which they use to choose and track improvements. It does not change appearance itself; it is a measuring stick that members use to set goals for skin, fitness, grooming and other changes.

infobox: 1 to 10, one step per tenth of the population [3]
Around 5 on decile; 4 on PSL per a forum rating guide [1]
Photo-rating apps exist for PSL-style scores [6]
Percentile, PSL, Chad, normie, sexual market value [2][7]

paras: A decile is any of the nine values that divide sorted data into ten equal parts, so each part holds a tenth of the sample [3]. Applied to attractiveness, a decile rank orders people from lowest to highest on a one-to-ten scale in which each successive number corresponds to an increase of ten percentage points of rank [3]. A person rated a 7 on the decile scale is described as sitting between roughly the 60th and 70th percentiles of the reference population.

Wikipedia contrasts this with the PSL scale, which it says typically runs from 1 to 8, measures only facial attractiveness, and sorts men into tiers from sub-3 through low-, mid- and high-tier normie to Chadlite, Chad and giga Chad [2]. Know Your Meme records the PSL ladder differently, as scores from 0 to 7.9 grouped into Subhuman, Sub 5, HTN/HTB, Chadlite or Stacylite, Chad or Stacy, and Adam or Eve, and notes that the community's claimed distribution, with most people between 1.5 and 5.5, cannot be measured [5]. Because tiers and cut-offs differ between sources, the translation between decile and PSL is a matter of forum convention rather than a fixed table.

Forum explanations treat both scales as roughly normal distributions. In the rating-guide thread, a reply states that the middle is 4 PSL, with one point up or down per step, and the original post says it gives members their percentile whenever it rates them because members are confused about how PSL maps onto the population [1].

Rating people on a scale of one to ten long predates looksmaxxing; Wikipedia notes that the PSL scale departs from the common x-out-of-ten convention [2]. PSL takes its name from three forums, PUAhate, Sluthate and Lookism, according to Wikipedia and Know Your Meme, and Wikipedia says looksmaxxing itself was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and popularised on TikTok in the 2020s [2][5]. Percentile and decile language entered these spaces as members tried to say how rare a given level of attractiveness is.

Related vocabulary reflects the same rank-based thinking. Wikipedia's article on the slang term Chad traces a 2000s Chicago usage and a 2010s internet one, and cites Angela Nagle in The Baffler in 2016 as placing Chads in the top decile of genetic fitness [7]. The incel version of the Pareto principle, the claim that 80 percent of women pursue the top 20 percent of men, is another way of stating a decile-style hierarchy; Wikipedia presents it as an incel assertion rather than an established finding, and notes that the Pareto principle itself is a rule of thumb about 80 percent of consequences coming from 20 percent of causes, credited to Vilfredo Pareto and popularised by Joseph Juran in 1941 [9][10].

By the 2020s such scales had spread beyond forums. Know Your Meme's entry on the PSL scale, created in February 2026, says short-form video and influencers such as Clavicular helped carry phrases like high PSL into wider use, often ironically [5]. A 2026 article by Gemma Ware for The Conversation, republished by the Cobb Courier, reports that PSL-style apps now rate uploaded photos and offer AI advice on how to move up the scale, sometimes for a fee, and that teenage boys often post photos on social media asking to be ranked [6].

Members use decile and percentile numbers in several ways. Rating threads invite a member to post photos and receive a rating, and the rating-guide author says he tells members their percentile when he rates them [1]. Comparison threads apply the scale to well-known people. Target-setting is the looksmaxxing use of the number: a member who places himself or herself in a given tenth of the population can discuss which changes, such as body fat, skin, grooming or surgery, might move the rating, and re-rate afterwards.

A guide shared on looksmax.org gives members percentile equivalents for PSL scores and describes how the average at 4 shifts as members compare against male models rather than the general public [1]. The rating-guide thread is itself titled as a request for an in-depth explanation of PSL and decile scales, which indicates that members ask how the two relate [1].

Social-science research uses 1-to-7 or 1-to-10 rating scales for attractiveness regularly, and Wikipedia's review of physical attractiveness collects findings relevant to them [8]. Panels of East Asian, Hispanic and White judges in Cunningham's work agreed substantially on which faces were attractive, and Cunningham in 1995 found that features associated with infants varied least across cultures in ratings [8]. Averageness, symmetry and sexual dimorphism are repeatedly linked to higher ratings: computer-averaged female faces were rated more attractive in a 2003 study by Murphy, and women were less attracted to men with asymmetrical faces in a 2002 study by Feng [8]. Dion, Berscheid and Walster (1972) described a halo effect in which attractive people are assumed to have other positive traits [8].

Population-level data from dating sites show how rank-like scoring can be derived from behaviour. Bruch and Newman's 2018 Science Advances study scored users from 0 (least desirable) to 1 (most desirable) using PageRank on messaging networks in New York, Boston, Chicago and Seattle, and found a clear hierarchy that was consistent across cities [4]. The authors note that this desirability score is a proxy inferred from who attracts messages and not a rating of attractiveness [4]. Wikipedia's article on online dating also summarises OkCupid analyses by Christian Rudder reporting that the most attractive male users, as rated by women, received about 11 times as many messages as the least attractive [11].

The matching hypothesis, first tested by Walster and colleagues in 1966 with 752 students at a computer dance, holds that people tend to pair with partners of similar attractiveness; later studies, such as one of 123 UCLA couples by White (1980), found similarly rated partners reported happier relationships, while Huston (1973) argued the pattern reflects avoidance of rejection [12]. Bruch and Newman describe a hybrid pattern in which users know roughly where they stand but still contact people above them, with replies becoming less likely as the gap widens [4].
No study has tested the specific conversions used in forums between PSL, decile and percentile, or the claim that most people fall in a stated range of PSL [5].

Wikipedia says sources describe the PSL scale as pseudoscientific [2]. Researchers Anda Iulia Solea and Lisa Sugiura, quoted by Know Your Meme, call PSL a systematic pseudoscientific framework that ranks people through a racialised and gendered hierarchy, and critics cited there argue that beauty is subjective and cannot be measured by geometry alone [5]. Jordan Foster, a sociology professor at MacEwan University interviewed by The Conversation, says the forums framed a taboo, feminised subject in the guise of science [6].

Supporters of rating, by contrast, point to the agreement among raters and to the fact that population percentiles give an intuitive sense of scale; decile scales are a statistical convention used in many fields, such as school socio-economic ranking in New Zealand, which Wikipedia lists as a related topic [3]. Wikipedia also notes that some incel forums are reported to harass users rated below average [2], and The Conversation's coverage links rating culture with concerns for parents of teenagers [6].
No studies found of the decile scale as used in looksmaxxing. Related research on attractiveness ratings, summarised above, uses similar numeric scales for different purposes.

timeline.event: Walster and colleagues run the Computer Match Dance, rating 752 students for attractiveness; the study founds the matching hypothesis [12].
Dion, Berscheid and Walster describe the attractiveness halo effect [8].
Cunningham reports cross-cultural agreement in attractiveness ratings for features linked to infants [8].
Looksmaxxing is coined on incel message boards, and PSL scales circulate through the PUAhate, Sluthate and Lookism forums [2][5].
Angela Nagle's article in The Baffler describes Chads as the top decile of genetic fitness [7].
Bruch and Newman publish a desirability hierarchy derived from dating-site messaging [4].
A looksmax.org guide gives PSL and percentile equivalents and states an average of 4 [1].
Journalists at the New York Times, Business Insider and Daily Dot cover looksmaxxing [2].
Know Your Meme documents the PSL scale and The Conversation reports on rating apps and influencers [5][6].

lore.intro: The decile scale appears in rating threads and explainer posts on looksmax.org, usually together with PSL [1].

claims.claim: Decile and PSL scores can be mapped onto each other
claims.believers: A rating-guide author converts PSL scores to percentiles and says average is 4, with each step a point up or down [1].
claims.experts: No published studies validate these conversions, and sources list different tier boundaries for PSL [5].

claims.claim: Attractiveness is normally distributed, so most people sit near the middle
claims.believers: Forum replies describe both scales as normal distributions with the middle at 4 PSL [1].
claims.experts: Rating-scale research uses the same assumption, but the PSL distribution cannot be measured according to Know Your Meme [5]; Rudder's OkCupid analyses show men's ratings of women looking roughly normal while women's ratings of men skewed lower [11].

claims.claim: A face or body can be rated objectively by strangers on a photo
claims.believers: Rating threads and apps present scores as meaningful snapshots of where someone stands [1][6].
claims.experts: Cunningham and others report substantial agreement among raters from different groups [8], while critics describe PSL-style scoring as pseudoscientific and subjective [5].

claims.claim: The top tenth of men receive most female attention (the 80/20 idea)
claims.believers: Incel and blackpill usage presents the 80/20 figure as a rule of dating markets [9].
claims.experts: Bruch and Newman found a long-tailed distribution of messages with a small group receiving very many [4]; Wikipedia presents the exact 80/20 figure as an incel assertion [9].

claims.claim: Knowing your decile helps you choose what to improve
claims.believers: Members use ratings from rating threads to decide which features to work on [1].
claims.experts: No published study has tested whether rating feedback leads to better outcomes; research on halo effects and averageness describes which traits influence ratings [8].

claims.claim: People tend to end up with partners in their own decile
claims.believers: Members who rate couples and celebrities by rank often discuss whether partners are matched or mismatched in score.
claims.experts: The matching hypothesis literature, from Walster in 1966 to White in 1980, reports partners of similar attractiveness tending to pair, with offsets such as wealth or status noted [12].
